text.p: Italy's information technology group Olivetti trimmed its losses in 1996 but still remained deep in the red and has resorted to reducing the nominal value of its shares as a possible method of raising fresh capital.

The group, which has not recorded a profit since 1990, reported on Tuesday that it had net losses in 1996 of 915 billion lire ($538 million), compared to 1.60 trillion lire of losses in 1995. Sales fell 14.6 percent to 8.30 trillion lire from 1995 levels.
A big loss was expected after the company based in Ivrea near Turin, northwest Italy, pointed to a 1996 pre-tax loss of 800 billion lire at the end of January.
The company said problems faced by the group had been exacerbated in the second half of 1996.

But the struggling group tried to paint a better picture for 1997, saying the company expected to approach break-even at the pre-tax level and before anticipated losses from its 35.5 percent stake in Italian mobile phone consortium Omnitel.

Olivetti said its first quarter of 1997 showed a pre-tax loss of 180 billion lire as sales slipped 10.4 percent to 1.38 trillion lire, but its net financial requirement rose sharply to 2.70 trillion lire from 2.20 trillion lire at the end of 1996.

The group said that its Q1 results were in line with its own internal budget while its key Olivetti Solutions-Olsy company, which makes computer systems for banks and retailers, had seen a significant sales recovery from the second half of 1996.
Q1 revenues were now in line with year earlier levels, it said.

Analysts had believed the company was comtemplating a reduction in the nominal share capital as a method of raising fresh capital by a rights issue which has been hinted at for the end of 1997. The share price took fright.

The shares rebounded up 4.54 percent at 554.6 lire on Tuesday ahead of the company releasing its results but the shares had fallen 5.73 percent on Monday and some feared they were heading towards the record low of 435 lire seen in October.

Olivetti raised a massive 2.26 trillion lire rights issue in late 1995 in a rescue act to relaunch the company, but the crisis simply deepened and those investors who subscribed at 1,000 lire a share saw the value of their holdings soon slump.

Olivetti struggled from crisis to crisis in 1996 seeing three chief executives over the year. Its chairman and biggest shareholder Carlo De Benedetti bowed out in September after he failed to reverse a series of losses and current chief executive Roberto Colaninno enacted his own rescue plan.

Colaninno has sold assets, such as the problematic personal computer company and a 5.6 percent stake in Omnitel, to keep long-suffering lending banks at bay, and has attempted to mould Olivetti into a telecoms and information technology group.

Olivetti said the 1996 net loss of 915 billion lire included provisions of 208.7 billion lire for "future expenses and risks" of which 59.5 billion lire was provided for first-quarter losses at Olivetti personal computers which the company finally sold at the beginning of April.
The group said gross margins declined from 1995 with the downturn stronger in the second half of 1996, particularly with regard to the profitability of personal computers and printers.

Second half problems were compounded as Olivetti director general Renzo Francesconi resigned and then cast doubts on the accuracy of the group's first half 1996 accounts, while magistrates and stock market watchdog Consob launched inquiries into the company's finances.

Colaninno's rescue plan calls for further asset sales in 1997, probably through the partial flotation of Olivetti's printer and fax company Lexikon on the U.S. market. He has said a rights issue may be needed at the end of 1997. ($1=1,700 lire)
